intro: Google lets you make up to three unsuccessful appeals for each disapproved Google Ad. After the third failed appeal, you must contact Google Ads support before you can appeal that ad again. This guide covers the limits, the steps in Policy manager on a Mac, and how to spend your tries well.

blocks.text: You can appeal a disapproved Google Ad up to three times without success. After the third unsuccessful appeal, you cannot appeal that ad again until you contact Google Ads support. The limit applies to each ad, not to your whole account, which matters when only one ad is blocked.
How the three-appeal limit works in Google Ads

Google's policy help says each ad can be appealed up to three times unsuccessfully. The word that matters is unsuccessfully. An appeal that succeeds is not a failed try. Count failed attempts ad by ad, not campaign by campaign.

items: Each ad allows up to three unsuccessful appeals in Policy manager.
After the third failed appeal, you contact Google Ads support for that ad.
Wait at least 24 hours between appeals on the same ads or campaigns.
The count belongs to the ad, so two ads have two separate counts.

blocks.title: Check the count first
blocks.text: Open the Appeal history tab before every new appeal. It lists each appealed ad, with the status and results of current and past appeals. If an ad already shows two failed appeals, your next try is the last one before support.
How to appeal in Google Ads Policy manager, step by step
Google Ads runs in your browser, so the steps happen in a web page on your Mac. Chrome is a safe choice. These are Google's steps for one ad, in order.

items: Open Google Ads and go to Tools > Troubleshooting > Policy manager.
On the Policy issues tab, find the disapproved ad.
Under Reason for appealing, choose Dispute decision or Made changes to comply with policy.
Add any note the form asks for, then select Submit.
Check the Appeal history tab once the review finishes.

blocks.text: For several ads you fixed at the same time, use the bulk path. Go to Campaigns > Ads, check each disapproved ad, select Edit, then choose Appeal policy decision. Pick the same reason options. Bulk appeals save clicks, but they spend a try on every ad you check, so select only the ads you have really changed.
Dispute decision or Made changes: which one to pick

Use Dispute decision when you think Google misread an ad that follows the policy. Use Made changes to comply with policy when you edited the ad or the page it links to. The reason should match what you actually did. A mismatch makes your appeal harder to follow. If it fails, it still counts against your three tries.

rows: Up to three. After that, contact Google Ads support for that ad.
At least 24 hours on the same ads or campaigns, to avoid duplicate marks.
From July 21, 2026, decisions more than six months old cannot be appealed in your account.
Most ads are reviewed within one business day, per Google's Search Ads 360 help page.

blocks.text: A worked example of the 24-hour rule

Say you file an appeal on Monday at 9 a.m. The earliest you can appeal that same ad again is Tuesday at 9 a.m. Most ads are reviewed within one business day, so the review may run alongside your wait. Three attempts need at least 48 hours of waiting between them, plus review time. Plan for days, not one afternoon, and start the first appeal early in the week.
What a disapproval costs in time and money

I found no public study that tracks how often marketers appeal, or how many appeals succeed. The cost you can measure is labor. The BLS puts the median pay for advertising, promotions, and marketing managers at $79.70 an hour, as of May 2025. That is a national median for the whole job group. At that rate, one hour of appeal work costs about $80 in labor. Use your own hourly cost if it differs.

The bigger cost is the ad that does not serve. A disapproved ad stays blocked until the review clears it. Each day it stays blocked is a day of lost clicks. Google's help pages do not put a figure on that. Pull the numbers from your own campaign reports before you decide how hard to fight for one ad.
How much to trust Google's accuracy claims

Google says its systems catch more than 99% of violating ads before they serve. It also says Gemini helped cut incorrect advertiser suspensions by 80% in 2025. Both are Google's own claims. I could not find an independent check that confirms them.

Google's numbers describe the whole system, not your account. Even a good system gets some ads wrong. Treat the accuracy claims as background. Your own disapproval reason and your own policy check should decide what you do next.

blocks.title: Do not spend a try on a guess
blocks.text: If you have not changed anything and cannot name the rule, read the policy first. An appeal with no real change still counts as an unsuccessful try. Fix the reason, then appeal.
Google Ads appeal history: read it before you file again

The Appeal history tab shows every appealed ad, with the status and results of current and past appeals. Open it before each new appeal, not after. Once a week, press ⌘ ⇧ 4, select the table, and save the image into your log folder. That gives you a dated record to share with your team or with support.
Mistakes people make with appeals

items: Appealing before changing anything, which spends a try for nothing.
Choosing Dispute decision on an ad that really broke the rule.
Filing again inside 24 hours, which can mark the appeal as a duplicate.
Trying to appeal a decision older than six months from inside the account.
Bulk-selecting a whole campaign when only a few ads changed.
Losing count, so the third failure arrives as a surprise.

blocks.text: When to contact Google Ads support instead of appealing

Stop appealing when an ad reaches three unsuccessful appeals. Google says you cannot appeal that ad again until you contact customer support. Contact support also when the decision is more than six months old. From July 21, 2026, you cannot appeal directly from your account for those decisions.

Support works better with a clean file. Bring the ad ID, the disapproval reason, every appeal date, the reason you picked each time, and what you changed. A timeline like that is easier for anyone to act on.
Client accounts and what you share with an AI tool

If the account belongs to a client, check your agency's data rules before you share screenshots or ad copy with any AI tool. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. It sends the audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer you. Lazur's privacy notes say those are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

Your employer's rules come first. Lawyers, nurses, accountants, and anyone under a client or patient data contract should ask before they share client details. When in doubt, hide the account name and customer data in the screenshot before you send it anywhere.
Where Lazur helps, and where it stops

Lazur can point at the Tools menu, explain a rejection in plain words, guide you one click at a time, and draft the appeal note for you to check. It can also set a reminder for your 24-hour check. It does not click Submit. It does not file appeals or change your ads, and it is not a plugin for Google Ads.

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and hold fn to dictate text at the cursor. Start at [the download page](/download), or see [pricing](/pricing) for plans.
How long Google Ads appeal review takes, and Editor on Mac
Google's Search Ads 360 help page says most ads are reviewed within one business day. Complex reviews take longer. If an ad is still under review after two full business days, check its status.

Google Ads Editor for Mac needs macOS 12 or later. Google's release page lists version 2.10, and newer builds may exist, so check the download page before you install. I did not confirm that Editor handles appeals. Use the browser steps above for now.

faq.question: How many times can you appeal a disapproved Google Ad?
faq.answer: Google's policy help says each ad can be appealed up to three times unsuccessfully. After that, you cannot appeal that ad again until you contact Google Ads support. The count is per ad, not per account.

faq.question: Does a successful appeal count toward the limit?
faq.answer: The limit is about unsuccessful appeals. A successful appeal is not a failed try. Still, check the Appeal history tab to see the result on each ad before you file again.

faq.question: How long do I need to wait between appeals?
faq.answer: Wait at least 24 hours between appeals for the same ads or campaigns. Google says this helps you avoid having them marked as duplicates.

faq.question: What if I cannot appeal from my account anymore?
faq.answer: From July 21, 2026, you cannot appeal directly from your account for policy decisions made more than six months earlier. For those, contact Google Ads support.

faq.question: How long does an appeal take to review?
faq.answer: Google's Search Ads 360 help page says most ads are reviewed within one business day. Complex reviews take longer. If an ad is still under review after two full business days, check its status.

faq.question: Can I appeal from Google Ads Editor on Mac?
faq.answer: Google Ads Editor for Mac needs macOS 12 or later, and Google's release page lists version 2.10. I did not confirm that Editor handles appeals. Google's appeal steps use the web interface, so use the browser.

faq.question: Where do I see the result of an appeal?
faq.answer: Open the Appeal history tab in Policy manager. It shows all appealed ads, with the status and results of current and past appeals.

faq.question: Will Lazur file the appeal for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points, explains, guides you one click at a time, and drafts text. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You press Submit yourself.

faq.question: Does a disapproval mean my ad broke the rule?
faq.answer: Not always. Google says its systems can flag nuanced cases for human review, and false flags do happen. Read the reason and the policy text before you decide whether to fix or dispute.

costs.title: Labor at the median rate
costs.text: The BLS median pay for advertising, promotions, and marketing managers is $79.70 an hour, from May 2025. That is a national median for the whole job group, not for PPC specialists alone. At that rate, each hour spent on appeals costs about $80 in labor. Multiply your own hours by your own rate.

costs.title: Lost ad delivery
costs.text: A disapproved ad does not serve while it is blocked. Each day it stays blocked is a day of lost clicks and sales that you cannot recover later. Google's help pages do not give a figure for that. Measure it from your own campaign data before you decide how hard to fight.

costs.title: Tries you cannot get back
costs.text: Each ad allows three unsuccessful appeals. A weak appeal filed in a hurry uses one of them. Once you reach three, you must contact support before you can appeal that ad again. Spend tries on real changes, not on guesses.

costs.title: Wait time between attempts
costs.text: Google asks for at least 24 hours between appeals on the same ads or campaigns. Three attempts need at least 48 hours of waiting between them, plus review time. A failed appeal late in the week can push your next try into the following week.

costs.title: Support escalation
costs.text: Once you reach the limit, or the decision is older than six months, you contact Google Ads support. That path is slower than an in-account appeal. The help pages in my research do not give a response time, so ask support for a timeline.

causes.title: Automated review flagged the ad
causes.text: Google uses automated systems to find ads that break its policies. Its Advertising Policies FAQ says it uses a combination of Google's AI and human evaluation to detect and remove violating ads. Automated checks are fast, and they can get edge cases wrong.

causes.title: A reviewer flagged a nuanced case
causes.text: The same FAQ says nuanced cases are flagged for trained operators and analysts. Those reviews take longer than the usual one business day, so the result can feel slow or random. The reason text still points to the policy you need to read.

causes.title: The landing page broke the rule
causes.text: An ad can be clean and still get disapproved because the page it links to breaks a policy. Open the destination page the way a visitor would, on a phone and on a Mac. Compare its claims with the ad text. Fix the page, then appeal with Made changes to comply with policy.

causes.title: A phrase triggered a restricted-content check
causes.text: Some words trigger checks on their own, even in an ordinary sentence. Compare each claim, product name, and superlative in the ad with the wording in the policy Google links to. Change the matching phrase, not the whole ad, when you can.

causes.title: A false flag
causes.text: False flags do happen. One PPC Hero writer describes a run of them and says a bug report sent through a dedicated rep stopped them on his account. That is one account, not a survey. Use it to appeal carefully, not as proof your ad is fine.

causes.title: You changed the ad, but not the cause
causes.text: Some appeals fail because the edit missed the rule. The reviewer sees the same problem again. Put the disapproval reason next to your edit, line by line. If the edit does not touch the flagged text or page, change that first.

fixes.title: Read the reason before you touch the ad
fixes.text: Hover over the Status column in Policy issues to see the reason. Click Read the policy under it. Note the exact rule, then search the policy page for the words that matter. A fix aimed at the wrong sentence wastes a try.

fixes.title: Fix the ad or page, then appeal as changed
fixes.text: If you changed the ad or the landing page, select Made changes to comply with policy. Describe the change in one plain line, such as removing a price claim from a headline. Keep that line in your log so you can repeat it on support requests.

fixes.title: Dispute only when Google misread a compliant ad
fixes.text: Use Dispute decision when the ad follows the policy and the review looks wrong. Quote the policy wording that supports you. If the ad does break the rule, a dispute will fail and still use a try.

fixes.title: Bulk appeal only the ads you fixed
fixes.text: Go to Campaigns > Ads, check each disapproved ad, select Edit, then Appeal policy decision. Check only the ads you actually fixed. Every checked ad uses a try if its appeal fails.

fixes.title: Keep a log in Google Sheets
fixes.text: Use one row per ad. Columns: ad ID, campaign, ad group, disapproval date, reason, appeal date, attempt number, result. Filter by attempt number to find ads with one or two tries left. Steps are in the [filter guide](/how-to/add-a-filter-to-a-range-in-google-sheets). For the wider sheet workflow, see [Google Sheets for marketers](/for/marketers/google-sheets).

fixes.title: Turn on disapproval alerts
fixes.text: Turn on Disapproved ads and policy alerts in your notification settings. PPC Hero recommends this setting in its write-up. You find out about a new disapproval sooner, so the fix starts sooner too.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Read the rejection and log it
plan.text: Open the ad in Policy issues and hover over the Status column. Click Read the policy under the reason. Log the ad ID, campaign, reason, and how many appeals you have already used. Do not appeal yet.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Fix the ad or the page
plan.text: Change the exact text or landing page the policy names. Take a screenshot with ⌘ ⇧ 4 before and after each change. Save both images in your log folder.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: File one appeal
plan.text: Go to Tools > Troubleshooting > Policy manager and select Appeal on the ad. Choose Made changes to comply with policy if you edited it, or Dispute decision if you did not. Submit once.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Check the result
plan.text: Open Appeal history for the ad. If it still shows disapproved, note the result and the time. Your next appeal must wait at least 24 hours from the last one.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Decide on the next try
plan.text: If you have two unsuccessful appeals, pause. Ask whether the change was real and matched the reason. File the third appeal only if you changed something new.

plan.label: Day 6
plan.title: Prepare a support request
plan.text: If you have three unsuccessful appeals, gather the ad ID, every appeal date, the reasons you picked, and the changes. Contact Google Ads support with that timeline.

plan.label: Day 7
plan.title: Set alerts and review the log
plan.text: Turn on Disapproved ads and policy alerts. Filter your sheet by result. Note which ads still have tries left, then plan the next week.
